newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha's image tarnished by Albanian crisis.
newsitem.headline: Berisha's image tarnished by Albanian crisis.

text.p: President Sali Berisha was the darling of the West in the early 1990s, respected for anchoring stability in Albania while the war in Bosnia threatened to ignite the Balkan tinderbox.

When he assumed power in April 1992, Sarajevo was about to suffer one of the bloodiest assaults on a European city since World War Two and hundreds of thousands of refugees were on the move from former Yugoslavia, which shared a border with Albania.

Berisha, a 52-year-old former university cardiologist, kept his cool, never failing to invoke his people to remain calm while ethnic Albanians over the border in Kosovo, in southern Yugoslavia, came under increasing threat from Belgrade.
The United States turned the once-Stalinist state into its closest ally in the region, sending over military advisers and aid.

Economically, Berisha was making all the right noises. A firm believer in the free market, the president won the confidence of foreign governments and international lending institutions over his plans to introduce real economic reform.

A fluent speaker of English and French, Berisha looked and sounded every bit the new Albanian leader, eager to embrace Western values and to push his country's case for closer ties with NATO and the European Union.

But Berisha is now facing the biggest crisis of his career, juggling the army's response to armed insurrection in the south of the country while trying to patch together a settlement with the political opposition to end the crisis.

He acknowledged his government had failed to take action quickly enough over the proliferation of pyramid investment schemes, despite warnings from the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund last year.

The demise of the shady savings funds and with them the meagre savings of thousands of Albanians have led to weeks of protests since January, escalating into anarchy last weekend in the towns of Vlore and Sarande.

Parliament declared an immediate state of emergency on Sunday, just hours before the chamber, mostly filled with Democratic Party MPs, elected Berisha to a second five-year term, a move criticised by the United States as inappropriate.
"He had a personal goal and he was not going to let anything get in the way of it. That was to be re-elected for another five years," a senior Western diplomat said.
Berisha co-founded the Democratic Party in December 1990 after a student uprising forced the Stalinist government of President Ramiz Alia to allow political parties and free elections.
He had worked inside a communist system that permitted him to study in France. But he has denied that he was a member of the medical team that administered to high-ranking leaders.
The Democrats plucked him from among a group of contenders to lead the party in 1991 before going on to win the 1992 general election by a landslide.
He rode a wave of popularity until a referendum in 1994 in which a small majority of Albanians rejected a draft constitution which would have given more power to the president.

Opposition parties say that was when the mood began to change. Amnesty International criticised the jailing of Socialist Party leader Fatos Nano, Berisha's main rival, on corruption charges. Washington did the same when supreme court chief Zef Brozi was sacked after saying Nano was innocent.

Last May's general election was widely criticised by foreign observers as failing to meet international standards. The polls were boycotted by the main opposition parties after they alleged voter intimidation and ballot stuffing.

Berisha's international standing was marred by the election and relations with Washington, which called for fresh polls at the earlier possible date, quickly cooled. No foreign government leader has paid Berisha a visit since the election, further evidence of the diplomatic cold shoulder.
His political survival and reputation will only be enhanced if he manages to pull off a political settlement while ending the southern uprising in as short a time as possible.
